findings.title: Async legacy writes are cancelled with the request
findings.body: Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection start the legacy write in a goroutine whose context is derived from the incoming request context via context.WithTimeoutCause (Create line 51, Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163). When the apiserver handler returns, that parent context is cancelled, which cancels the child immediately. The 10s timeout never applies, and Legacy.Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection observe context.Canceled instead of finishing. Mode 3's legacy copy therefore does not land on the success path, so a rollback to legacy storage loses or stale-reads every write that was acknowledged from unified storage.

findings.title: Per-object legacy writes are unordered
findings.body: Each successful Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection fires an independent goroutine with no per-key queue, lock, or generation check. The handler returns as soon as unified storage succeeds, so a later delete (or newer update) can be applied to legacy before the earlier create/update. Legacy can then contain a resurrected object or an older spec while unified storage, which mode 3 reads, has the new state. Rollback or any legacy reader then serves data the API already deleted or overwrote. The closure also shares the request object with the caller; if Storage.Create returns that same pointer, the caller's continued use races with Legacy.Create.

findings.title: Legacy update no longer persists the unified result
findings.body: Update now passes the original objInfo into Legacy.Update after Storage.Update returns. The previous implementation computed the object once from unified storage and wrote that exact result to legacy through updateWrapper. In mode 3 the client resourceVersion comes from unified storage, so legacy GuaranteedUpdate's optimistic check fails with a conflict once the two backends' resource versions differ, and the safety copy is dropped. Even if legacy ignores resourceVersion, UpdatedObject runs against legacy's own old object and can persist a different spec. objInfo is also not guaranteed to be reusable after the first Update, so the async second call can fail or write a mutated object.

findings.title: NotFound on unified delete skips legacy cleanup
findings.body: Delete returns on any Storage.Delete error, including NotFound, and never starts the legacy delete. The previous mode 3 delete still removed the object from legacy when unified storage returned NotFound. During migration, legacy can still hold objects that unified storage does not. Those deletes now fail to the client and leave the legacy row in place, so a fallback to legacy resurrects objects the API reported as gone.

findings.title: Successful delete records the object name as the kind label
findings.body: On a successful Storage.Delete, recordStorageDuration is called with the object name as the third argument. Every other call in this file passes options.Kind. If that argument is a Prometheus label, every distinct deleted name becomes a new series. That grows without bound for the process registry and any scraper, and the delete latency/error series can no longer be aggregated by kind.

findings.title: Storage and legacy durations are recorded on the wrong series
findings.body: When Storage.Create fails, line 45 calls recordLegacyDuration for a unified-storage failure, and Update does the same at line 129 with recordLegacyDuration. DeleteCollection's async legacy call at line 166 calls recordStorageDuration, so the legacy outcome is counted as another storage observation and legacy delete-collection latency is never recorded. Alerts and dashboards for mode 3 will attribute unified-storage failures to legacy and hide real legacy delete-collection failures.

findings.title: Legacy write failures are not logged
findings.body: The async Legacy.Create, Legacy.Update, Legacy.Delete, and Legacy.DeleteCollection calls only feed a boolean into the duration metric. The previous synchronous path logged the legacy error with the object identity. A timeout, conflict, or context cancellation now leaves unified storage and legacy diverged with no log line, so the safety copy can fail indefinitely without an operator-visible signal.

findings.title: Destroy does not wait for in-flight legacy writes
findings.body: Destroy closes Storage and Legacy immediately, but Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection do not track their goroutines. Shutdown can destroy legacy storage while a goroutine is still inside Legacy.Create/Update/Delete, which races with teardown and drops the safety copy for writes that were already acknowledged. There is no WaitGroup or drain anywhere in DualWriterMode3.

findings.title: Mode 3 tests never wait for or assert the legacy write
findings.body: Success-path tests install legacy On expectations (Create around line 31, Update around line 313) but return as soon as the synchronous unified call finishes, and they never call AssertExpectations or wait for the goroutine. testify will not fail if the legacy call is skipped, and the goroutine can invoke the mock after the test has finished. Both stores also share one mock.Mock, so a single Create/Update expectation cannot prove which backend ran. The new cases in pkg/tests/apis/playlist/playlist_test.go (file mode 3 at line 132, unified mode 3 at line 191) call doPlaylistTests, which immediately lists and gets the legacy playlist API after a k8s write. Those checks assume the legacy write is synchronous; with this mode 3 they race, and they fail outright if the request context cancels the legacy write.
